summary: Specifies BGPsec, an extension to BGP that secures the AS path in UPDATE messages. Each AS that passes on the message adds a digital signature in an optional non-transitive path attribute, which shows that every AS on the path authorized the advertisement.

eli5.summary: Each stop on a trip stamps the passport so you can check the route claimed is the real route.

questions: how does bgpsec validate the as path
what does pcount 0 mean in bgpsec
subtitle: Digital signatures on every hop of a BGP route, so a receiver can check the AS path was really passed along.

tldr.problem: BGP UPDATE messages carry an AS path that nothing protects, so a receiver cannot tell whether each AS on the path really chose to pass the route on.
tldr.mechanism: Each AS that forwards a route to an external peer adds a digital signature covering the prefix, the path so far and the next AS, carried in a new optional non-transitive BGPsec_PATH attribute that replaces AS_PATH. A receiver checks the signatures against keys from RPKI router certificates.
tldr.outcome: A valid message proves the UPDATE travelled along the listed ASes, though not that data packets follow that path. It is updated by RFC 8206.

today: RFC 8205 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, but it is updated by RFC 8206.

sections.title: What BGPsec Adds to BGP
sections.content:
BGPsec gives path security to BGP route advertisements. A BGP speaker that receives a valid BGPsec UPDATE message has cryptographic assurance that every Autonomous System (AS) on the listed path explicitly authorized the advertisement of the route to the next AS in the path.

It is carried in a new optional, non-transitive path attribute, BGPsec_PATH. BGPsec is meant to supplement BGP origin validation (RFC 6483, RFC 6811); used together, they can prevent a wide variety of route hijacking attacks.

It depends on the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI). A speaker that wants to send BGPsec UPDATEs to external peers needs a private key tied to an RPKI router certificate for its AS number. Validating received messages does not require such a certificate.
sections.eli5: Each router signs for the part of the trip it handled, and the keys to check those signatures come from an official list of who owns which network.

sections.title: Negotiating BGPsec
sections.content:
BGPsec defines a BGP capability with code 7 and a length of 3 octets. The first 4 bits give the version (only version 0 is defined), the fifth bit is a Direction bit (0 means able to receive, 1 means able to send) and the last 3 bits are unassigned. The next two octets are the Address Family Identifier, and the RFC specifies BGPsec only for IPv4 (AFI 1) and IPv6 (AFI 2).

A peer may send BGPsec UPDATEs only if it advertised the send direction and the other side advertised the receive direction for the same version and address family. To do both, a speaker sends two copies of the capability. A speaker MUST NOT advertise BGPsec for an AFI unless it also advertised the multiprotocol extension for that AFI, and any speaker announcing BGPsec MUST also announce 4-byte AS number support.

Ordinary unsigned UPDATEs may still be sent whether or not BGPsec was negotiated, but BGPsec UPDATEs MUST NOT be sent if it was not.
sections.eli5: Before sending signed mail, both sides say whether they can send it, receive it, or both. Signed mail only flows when one side can send and the other can receive.

sections.title: The BGPsec_PATH Attribute
sections.content:
BGPsec_PATH replaces AS_PATH: an UPDATE with one MUST NOT contain the other. It has a Secure_Path, logically the same information as an AS_PATH, followed by one or two Signature_Blocks. Two blocks (one per algorithm suite) are used only during a transition from an old algorithm suite to a new one.

The Secure_Path starts with a 2-octet length and then holds one 6-octet Secure_Path Segment per AS. Each segment has a pCount (1 octet), a flags octet whose top bit is the Confed_Segment flag, and a 4-octet AS number. pCount is the number of repetitions of that AS the signature covers, which mimics prepending without extra signatures. Summing the pCount values gives the AS path length.

Each Signature_Block has a 2-octet length, a 1-octet Algorithm Suite Identifier and one Signature Segment per Secure_Path Segment. A Signature Segment holds a 20-octet Subject Key Identifier (SKI) naming the router certificate to verify with, a 2-octet signature length and the signature itself.
sections.eli5: The attribute is a list of stops on the route, plus a matching list of signed stamps, one stamp per stop.

sections.title: Sending: Building and Signing
sections.content:
A BGPsec UPDATE MUST advertise only one prefix, and it MUST use MP_REACH_NLRI to encode it. Because the signature includes the AS number of the peer it is sent to, a separate message is needed for each distinct peer AS.

When forwarding to an external peer, a speaker prepends a new Secure_Path Segment with its own AS number, which MUST match the Subject of its RPKI router certificate, and a new Signature Segment. The signature covers, in this exact order, the target AS number, the earlier signature and path segments, the algorithm suite identifier, the AFI, the SAFI and the NLRI. That sequence is hashed with the suite's digest algorithm and then signed. Toward internal peers the attribute SHALL NOT be modified.

A route server that is not a transit AS in the data plane may set pCount to 0, and still adds its AS number. Members of an AS confederation use pCount 0 and the Confed_Segment flag for member-AS hops, and strip those segments when the route leaves the confederation. A speaker producing an UPDATE that would contain an AS_SET MUST NOT include BGPsec_PATH. If a peer does not support BGPsec, the AS_PATH is rebuilt from the Secure_Path and an unsigned UPDATE is sent.
sections.eli5: Each router signs a stamp that names who it is handing the letter to and includes all earlier stamps, so nobody can swap in a different route afterwards.

sections.title: Receiving: Validation
sections.content:
A speaker SHOULD validate BGPsec UPDATEs received from external peers. First it checks the message is well formed: the attribute is syntactically correct, the newest AS matches the peer's AS in the OPEN message, each Signature_Block has one segment per Secure_Path Segment, no AS_PATH is present, Confed_Segment and pCount values are acceptable for that peer, and the local AS is not in the path. Errors are handled with treat-as-withdraw from RFC 7606.

Then, for each Signature_Block with a supported algorithm suite, it checks segments from the newest to the oldest. It finds a matching (AS number, public key, SKI) from valid RPKI router certificates, rebuilds the same hashed octet sequence, and verifies the signature. One bad signature marks the whole block 'Not Valid'. The message is 'Valid' if at least one block is 'Valid'.

What to do with the result is local policy. Validity depends on current RPKI state, so affected messages in the Adj-RIB-In MUST be revalidated when it changes.
sections.eli5: The receiver checks the stamps one by one starting with the latest. If one is fake, the whole set fails.

sections.title: Algorithms, Operations and Partial Deployment
sections.content:
Algorithm choice is not negotiated per peer, because every speaker the route eventually reaches must understand it. RFC 8208 sets a mandatory 'current' suite, and a future transition would carry signatures for both suites. When a speaker supports only one of two blocks, it removes the other. A 'Not Valid' block MUST NOT be removed when propagating, so downstream entities are not tricked into treating the route as unsigned.

Operational points include logging failed negotiation, configuring who may use pCount 0, using local RPKI views for private AS numbers, and, for ECDSA with curve P-256, generating a fresh high-entropy secret number for every signature.

During partial deployment, if an AS on the path does not support BGPsec, the message is converted to an unsigned UPDATE before forwarding, and the assurance stops at that point. Early adopters get protection within contiguous groups of BGPsec ASes.
sections.eli5: If one stop on the route cannot read signed stamps, the letter loses its stamps there, so the proof only covers the part of the trip before that stop.

sections.title: Security Guarantees and Limits
sections.content:
Together with origin validation, a valid message shows that the origin AS was authorized by the address space holder, and that each AS in the path intentionally chose to propagate the route to the next. BGPsec does not guarantee that data packets follow the indicated path, only that the UPDATE did. A speaker's signature does not attest that earlier signatures were valid.

Limits listed in the RFC: a 'Not Valid' status can differ between vantage points because RPKI data differs; setting pCount to 0 could be abused to attract traffic, which operational guidance largely mitigates; colluding ASes can tunnel signed messages; replay attacks, where a withdrawn announcement is replayed, are addressed by router certificate rollover; and BGPsec does not protect the transport layer, so sessions SHOULD use transport security.

For denial-of-service resistance, cheap checks come before signature checks, and verification stops at the first invalid signature.
sections.eli5: The stamps prove the letter was handed along the claimed route, not that the trucks later drive that way.

fields.name: Version
fields.desc: BGPsec version; only version 0 is defined.

fields.name: Dir
fields.desc: 0 means able to receive BGPsec UPDATEs, 1 means able to send.

fields.name: Unassigned
fields.desc: Set to 0 by the sender and ignored by the receiver.

fields.name: AFI
fields.desc: Address family: 1 for IPv4, 2 for IPv6.

fields.name: pCount
fields.desc: Repetitions of this AS number that the signature covers.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Top bit is Confed_Segment; the other 7 bits are unassigned and MUST be 0.

fields.name: AS Number
fields.desc: AS of the speaker that added this segment.
